title: Seven baskets (Mark 8:1–10)
hookLine: a second feeding, in Gentile country, four thousand fed
last: EPHPHATHA — A SOUND YOU USUALLY IGNORE.

cards: Ever had déjà vu so strong you almost laughed? A huge crowd, out in the middle of nowhere. Nothing to eat.

Jesus turns to the disciples and says, I feel for these people. And the disciples, who watched five thousand fed from five loaves just two chapters ago, ask where anyone could find bread out here. You want to shake them.
Then again, how often does anyone forget what already happened to them?

teach.h: THREE DAYS, AND NOTHING TO EAT.
teach.b: This time Jesus speaks first, in the old King James Bible: "I have compassion on the multitude, because they have now been with me three days, and have nothing to eat." They've stayed so long their food ran out.
Some, he says, came from far away; send them home hungry and they'll collapse on the road. The disciples answer: "From whence can a man satisfy these men with bread here in the wilderness?"
He asks the same question as before: what have you got? Seven loaves, and a few small fish. He has everyone sit on the ground, gives thanks, breaks, and hands it to the disciples to give out.

The Greek for gave thanks is the word that gives us eucharist, the name many churches use for communion. Four thousand eat and are satisfied, and seven baskets are left over. Why tell a second feeding at all?
Look at the map. Yesterday Jesus was in the ten cities, Gentile country. Many readers think this crowd is mostly Gentile, the same people the Syrophoenician mother spoke for.

The first time, twelve baskets, like the twelve tribes of Israel. This time, seven, a number of fullness and completeness, and some hear the nations in it. The crumbs she asked for became a meal with leftovers.
Even the baskets are different. The first feeding used a Greek word for a small wicker basket; this one uses a word for a big one, large enough, in Acts, to lower Paul over a city wall.
Then they sail off to a place called Dalmanutha.
Nobody today knows where that was.

how: Many churches call communion the Eucharist, from the Greek word for giving thanks, and many Christians volunteer at food banks and shared meals that feed people beyond their own congregation.

games.why: from whence can a man satisfy these men with bread here in the wilderness? they'd forgotten. he fed them anyway.

practice: Picture the people you feed without thinking, family, friends, the office birthday, then look just past the edge of that circle: a neighbor you don't know, a coworker from another team, a stranger at a shelter or a food bank who's been waiting a while and came from far.
Choose one way you could feed someone outside your circle. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you have, the way he did before he broke the bread.

wordCard.voice: Seven baskets. The leftovers from a second feeding, four thousand, in Gentile country, enough again.
